extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, petitioners, and practitioners (patent attorneys/agents) participating in AIA trial proceedings before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_short: motions to amend in PTAB trials
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural standards governing motions to amend (MTAs), preliminary guidance, revised MTAs, burdens of persuasion, evidentiary scope, and related timing/extensions in AIA trial proceedings before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original motion to amend — filing timing and conferral requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may file one original motion to amend a patent, but only after conferring with the Board. Unless a due date is provided in a Board order, an original motion to amend must be filed no later than the filing of a patent owner response. If a patent owner wishes to receive preliminary guidance from the Board, the original motion to amend must include the patent owner's request for that preliminary guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines when an original MTA is timely and requires conferral with the Board before filing; if preliminary guidance is desired it must be requested in the original MTA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope — grounds for denial of a motion to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Any motion to amend may be denied where: (i) The amendment does not respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial; or (ii) The amendment seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion amendments must be responsive to grounds actually in the trial and cannot enlarge claim scope or add new matter; these are explicit bases for denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable number of substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Any motion to amend may cancel a challenged claim or propose a reasonable number of substitute claims. The presumption is that only one substitute claim will be needed to replace each challenged claim, and it may be rebutted by a demonstration of need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a default presumption (one-for-one) as to replacement claims; parties may rebut by showing need for additional substitute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for motions to amend (claim listing and support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any motion to amend claims must include a claim listing, which claim listing may be contained in an appendix to the motion, show the changes clearly, and set forth: (1) The support in the original disclosure of the patent for each proposed substitute claim; and (2) The support in an earlier-filed disclosure for each claim for which the benefit of the filing date of the earlier-filed disclosure is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions must clearly show amendments and provide explicit written-description and priority/benefit support; claim listings may be in an appendix but must show changes clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional motion to amend — authorization and good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as provided for revised motions, any additional motion to amend may not be filed without Board authorization. An additional motion to amend may be authorized when there is a good cause showing or a joint request of the petitioner and the patent owner to materially advance a settlement. In determining whether to authorize such an additional motion to amend, the Board will consider whether a petitioner has submitted supplemental information after the time period set for filing a motion to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional MTAs (beyond original and the one revised MTA exception) require Board permission based on good cause or settlement considerations; late supplemental petitioner information is a factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner's burden of persuasion on motions to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies with the requirements of paragraphs (1) and (3) of 35 U.S.C. 316(d) (or 326(d)), as well as the rule's scope/content requirements (e.g., not enlarging claims, not introducing new matter, showing support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners must prove, by preponderance, statutory and regulatory compliance for MTAs (written-description, no new matter, limitation to responding grounds, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner's burden of persuasion on substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must prove unpatentability of proposed substitute claims by preponderance; this is explicit allocation under the burden-allocation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion — interests of justice and evidence the Board may consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrespective of the burden allocations, the Board may exercise its discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend or raise a new ground of unpatentability in connection with a proposed substitute claim. Where the Board exercises this discretion, the parties will have notice and an opportunity to respond. In exercising this discretion the Board may consider all evidence of record in the proceeding and may consider and make of record: (i) any evidence in a related proceeding before the Office and evidence that a district court can judicially notice; and (ii) when no petitioner opposes or all petitioners cease to oppose a motion to amend, prior art identified through a prior art search conducted by the Office at the Board's request. The request for and the results of such a prior art search will be made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board retains broad, discretionary authority ('interests of justice') to act beyond party-introduced evidence in limited circumstances, but must provide notice and opportunity to respond. The rule clarifies what outside evidence (related proceedings, judicial notice, Office prior-art search results) the Board may consider/make of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination standard when Board raises its own ground of unpatentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Board exercises its discretion to raise a new ground of unpatentability in connection with a proposed substitute claim, the Board must determine unpatentability based on a preponderance of the evidence of record or made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for Board-raised grounds, the standard for finding unpatentability is a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary guidance — request, content, and nonbinding status
rubrics_metrics.description: In its original motion to amend, a patent owner may request that the Board provide preliminary guidance setting forth the Board's initial, preliminary views on the original motion to amend, including whether the parties have shown a reasonable likelihood of meeting their respective burdens of persuasion and notice of any new ground of unpatentability discretionarily raised by the Board. Any preliminary guidance will not be binding on the Board in any subsequent decision, is not a 'decision' under § 42.71(d), and is not subject to rehearing or Director review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary guidance is an optional, non-binding initial assessment by the Board intended to indicate reasonable-likelihood issues and any discretionary new grounds; it is procedural, not final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary guidance — timing, scope, and what it addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's preliminary guidance typically will come after a petitioner's opposition (or after the opposition due date if none is filed) and will provide at minimum an initial discussion about whether there is a reasonable likelihood that the original MTA meets statutory/regulatory requirements and whether the petitioner or the record establishes a reasonable likelihood that the substitute claims are unpatentable. The preliminary guidance may also address new grounds of unpatentability discretionarily raised by the Board, together with citations to the evidence of record supporting those new grounds. Generally, it will address proposed substitute claims in the original MTA and will not address patentability of the originally challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary guidance is targeted at the substitute claims and whether parties appear likely to meet burdens; it may cite record evidence and identify discretionary new grounds, but is not exhaustive nor binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on replies, sur-replies, and new evidence in the MTA process
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner's reply or a revised MTA may be accompanied by new evidence. New evidence (including declarations) may be submitted with every paper in the MTA process, except with a sur-reply or in a special circumstance discussed. The sur-reply may respond to the preliminary guidance and is limited to responding to arguments made in the patent owner's reply brief, to commenting on reply declaration testimony, or pointing to cross-examination testimony, and may not be accompanied by new evidence. If a patent owner does not file either a reply or a revised MTA after receiving preliminary guidance, a petitioner may file a reply to the preliminary guidance, but such a reply may respond only to the preliminary guidance and may not be accompanied by new evidence; a patent owner may then file a sur-reply, also without new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can file new evidence widely, but sur-replies are tightly limited: no new evidence and limited scope; special rules apply when patent owner takes no action following preliminary guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised motion to amend — one revised MTA without prior authorization and replacement rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrespective of the additional-motion restriction, a patent owner may, without prior authorization from the Board, file one revised motion to amend after receiving an opposition to the original motion to amend or after receiving the Board's preliminary guidance. A revised motion to amend must be responsive to issues raised in the preliminary guidance or in the petitioner's opposition and must include one or more new proposed substitute claims in place of the previously presented substitute claims, where each new proposed substitute claim presents a new claim amendment. If filed, the revised motion to amend replaces the original motion to amend in the proceeding. A patent owner may not incorporate by reference substitute claims or arguments presented in the original MTA into the revised MTA; all proposed substitute claims a patent owner wishes the Board to consider must be presented in the revised MTA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule formalizes the pilot-program practice that allows one self-authorized revised MTA that (1) replaces the original, (2) must present new claim amendments responsive to issues raised, and (3) cannot simply incorporate earlier material by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence (declarations) — deposition availability expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing new declarations, parties are expected to make their declarants available for depositions promptly and to make their attorneys available to take and defend such depositions; any unavailability will not be a reason to adjust the schedule for briefing on an MTA or revised MTA absent extraordinary circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting declaration evidence implicates depositions and the schedule; parties should plan for prompt deposition availability and cannot rely on unavailability to extend MTA briefing timelines except in extraordinary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board solicitation of examination assistance / prior art searches and making results of record
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may solicit patent examiner assistance in the MTA context, including requesting that the Office conduct a prior art search. The proposed rule clarifies that a Board request for a prior art search and the results of such a search by the Office will be made of record. The Board has not historically solicited such examination assistance frequently, but the rule explicitly authorizes and requires making any such search request and results part of the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies procedure and record-making when the Board uses Office resources (examiner/advisory reports or prior art searches) to evaluate MTAs, particularly where petitioners do not oppose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of deadlines and final written decision for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director (delegated to the Chief Administrative Patent Judge) has discretion to extend the deadline for issuing a final written decision for good cause and by not more than 6 months. The Board may determine whether to grant extensions of other deadlines under § 42.5(c)(2) after conference with the parties. Examples of good cause include complex issues, unavailability of the panel, or the need to accommodate additional papers (such as additional briefing or an Office prior art search report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions beyond default MTA timelines are possible but reserved for good cause; the Chief APJ must authorize extensions of the final written decision date beyond one year (up to six months). The Board typically considers extensions after consultation with parties.
